**Tuesday 3 Nov — AI + cyber (876 chars)**

```
Hackers raised the temperature in hundreds of supermarket fridges overnight. The food spoiled. In some stores it caught fire.

The controllers were reachable from the open internet. One flaw let an attacker log in as an administrator using a code derived from the current date, without the password. The fix had been available for over a year.

Misconfiguration is not a new problem. It has sat on the OWASP Top 10 since 2004, under one name or another. The 2025 edition found some form of it in every application tested.

A default password, an exposed management page, a service nobody turned off. None of these require a novel exploit. They require someone to leave the door open.

The oldest issues are the ones we still walk through.

What is the simplest misconfiguration you have found in a real system?

#CyberSecurity #Misconfiguration #OTSecurity #InfoSec #CyberRisk
```

**Fact basis (sources stay out of the post body):**
- **UK impact** — BBC 3 Nov: NCSC aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK." The Grocer 3 Nov: a wholesaler had 6 of 10 cold-room controllers hacked, max temperature set to 150ºF, automated temperature warnings disabled.
- **Open internet exposure** — Censys 14 Oct: 1,825 controllers exposed in France on 11 Oct, down to 537 by 14 Oct. The date-derived admin login (CVE-2025-41450) was disclosed March 2025 and fixed in firmware 4.2.
- **OWASP history** — Top 10 first released 2003, updated 2004 and 2007. "Insecure Configuration Management" was A10 in 2004, dropped 2007, returned as "Security Misconfiguration" in 2010. The 2025 edition found some form of misconfiguration in 100% of tested applications, over 719,000 CWE occurrences.

No company names, no countries, no towns in the body. Topic is fresh against the 17-topic registry.

---

I handle around four to five access requests daily, checking business approval and documenting the access period. I treat the end date as part of the request, because approving access includes deciding how long it is needed.

I think of time limited permissions like lending someone a key for a particular job. I want the person to have access to what they need, with a clear point to review whether they still need it.

I document extensions too, so I can explain why an access period changed. I find that a useful test of my own judgement, could I explain the permission from the record alone.

I want to become someone colleagues can depend on for these everyday decisions. I would like to know, how do you decide when temporary access deserves an extension?

#CyberSecurity #AccessControl #IdentityAndAccessManagement #ITSupport #LeastPrivilege

You can approve the text now. Publication will wait for the factual checks.

**Friday 6 Nov — AI + non-cyber (923 chars)**

```
A startup just came out of stealth with $62.5 million to build a world model that predicts how a person will behave.

Not what they will buy. How they will decide.

It reads sentiment, voice, how often someone calls support, the timing of transfers. It converts those into a mathematical picture of a person, then estimates the probability of their next choice.

The company says it is running this at a handful of brokerages, to anticipate how traders act when markets turn volatile.

I keep thinking about the phrase "every individual is the world." A world model is supposed to simulate a place. This one simulates a person.

The company is candid that the claim is probabilistic, not certain. That is honest. But a probability about a person is still a claim about who they are.

What would you want to know before a model made that kind of claim about you?

#AI #WorldModel #Privacy #DataEthics #ArtificialIntelligence
```
